summary: Olympic National Forest L-4 cab built 1939, abandoned as a lookout in 1969, later used for radio; reached by a forest road and a walk past a closed gate.

facts.status_note: No longer used as a lookout; converted to radio communication. The register still counts the building as a standing structure.

access.note: Reached by a forest road and then a walk past a closed gate. The building is used for radio communication, and no source describes public entry.

visit.trail_note: Drive Forest Road 3041 to the Kloshe Nanich former lookout site, then walk about half a mile up the road past a closed gate. TrailChick advises high clearance.

facts.agency: US Forest Service - Olympic National Forest

events.note: L-4 cab built in 1939; the register, TrailChick and firelookout.com agree.
A federal survey record names a North Point Lookout House with a 1954 designation, which suggests the building was standing by then.
Manned on an emergency basis, per a May 1956 Port Angeles newspaper item.
Bryon Loucks observed and reported fires from the lookout.
After abandonment the cab was converted to radio or communication use; the sources do not give a date for the change.
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register on April 13, 2022.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register gives 3,348 ft (1,020 m) and TrailChick gives 3,320 ft. The record's 1020.5 m matches the register.
The register says the cab became a communication tower and firelookout.com says a radio communication building. Both describe radio or communication use, so the record's standing status stands.

notes_for_editor: Sparse history: the 1939 build year agrees across three sources, but no Forest Service primary record was read. Newspaper items come via the Forest Lookouts of Washington page, not the original papers. A search hit (willhite site) suggested extra detail but was not read, so it is not cited. Elevation differs by about 28 ft between the register and TrailChick. The register and firelookout.com differ on the post-1969 use. No new photos.
